title: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Despite pi's simple definition, its digit sequence shows no significant regularity in all computed digits and appears for practical purposes completely random.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Despite the simplicity of its definition, the digit sequence of π seems for practical purposes completely random.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Mathematical Constants” (from p. 136), p. 138. Scope: digit sequence of pi in any base

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.87

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Enormous digit samples and standard statistical tools are publicly available, making practical finite-scale regularity highly testable. The universal absence of significant regularity and all-base wording remain beyond finite evidence.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Apply preregistered frequency, run, correlation, spectral, and compression tests to very large published or reproducibly computed digit blocks of pi in several bases. Any significant stable regularity refutes the practical claim under those tests; failure to detect one supports but cannot prove complete randomness.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No finite test establishes complete randomness or absence of every significant regularity.

Normality of pi is unproved.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.96
data existence: 1.0
operationalizability: 0.78
discriminating power: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Wolfram's claim is explicitly about computed digits and practical randomness, and public archives now hold many orders of magnitude more digits than the two hundred billion he cites. Running standard tests on those digits, or inspecting the published tests, can confirm the practical claim or refute it by exhibiting a regularity. Normality of pi remains unproved, and that is a stronger statement than the one being scored.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Apply a fixed suite of normality and randomness tests to public prefixes of the digits of pi in several bases. A significant regular pattern on those prefixes would refute the practical claim; continued absence of such a pattern on prefixes far larger than those Wolfram cites would confirm it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Passing statistical tests on a finite prefix does not prove that pi is normal.

A regularity with an extremely long period can be missed by any fixed test suite.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.95
analysis feasibility: 0.85
operationalizability: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.65

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: The first 1,000,000 decimal and the first 1,000,000 hexadecimal digits of pi after the point show no statistically significant regularity under a fixed battery of frequency, block, poker, gap, serial-correlation, spectral and compression tests, i.e. they are indistinguishable from i.i.d. uniform digits by these tests.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py computes pi to 1,000,020 digits in base 10 and in base 16 by the Chudnovsky series with exact integer binary splitting (28 s), downloads the published 1,000,000-digit decimal file and the OEIS b-files and compares them digit by digit with the computation, then runs the pre-registered ten-test battery in each base on the first 10^6 digits after the point: chi-square tests of digit, non-overlapping pair and triple frequencies, a 5-digit poker test, a gap test for digit 0, serial correlations at lags 1-3, a maximum-periodogram test and an lzma size comparison with 20 PRNG digit strings. The 20 p-values are counted against the pre-registered thresholds.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. For each base b in {10, 16}, on N = 1,000,000 digits after the point, compute 10 p-values: (1) digit frequency chi-square (b - 1 df); (2) non-overlapping pair chi-square (b^2 - 1 df); (3) non-overlapping triple chi-square (b^3 - 1 df); (4) poker test on non-overlapping 5-digit hands by number of distinct digits (probabilities b!/(b-r)! S(5, r) / b^5; categories with expected count < 5 merged into the next); (5) gap test for digit 0 (gap lengths 0..3b-1 and >= 3b against the geometric law with p = 1/b); (6-8) serial correlation at lags 1, 2, 3 (z = r sqrt(N - lag), two-sided normal); (9) maximum periodogram ordinate of the centred digits over the N/2 Fourier frequencies (p = 1 - (1 - exp(-max I / mean I))^(N/2)); (10) lzma (preset 9 extreme) size of the digit string (one byte per digit) compared with 20 strings of N uniform random digits from numpy PCG64 (seed 20261031): two-sided normal p of z = (size - mean) / sd. 20 p-values in total. 'supports' if no p-value is below 1e-4 and at most 2 are below 0.01 (under the null, P(>= 3 of 20 below 0.01) is about 0.1 %). Data validity: the published decimal digits must agree with digits computed independently by analysis.py (Chudnovsky series, exact integer arithmetic) at all 1,000,000 positions, and with the OEIS A000796 b-file; the computed hexadecimal digits must agree with the OEIS A062964 b-file. Any disagreement makes the verdict 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any p-value is below 1e-6 or 4 or more p-values are below 0.01. Otherwise, if neither the pass nor the refute condition holds (exactly 3 below 0.01, or a minimum p in [1e-6, 1e-4)), 'mixed'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: p-values of the pre-registered battery (minimum: maximum-periodogram test, base 16)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: deterministic digits; p-values are the tests' own (asymptotic chi-square / normal approximations); the lzma p-value depends on the 20-sample PRNG reference

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'For practical purposes completely random' is read as: a standard battery of statistical tests of the kind used to vet random number generators finds no significant regularity. The claim's scope is 'any base'; bases 10 and 16 are tested (base 2 is tested separately in wolfram2002-ch10-15). Wolfram refers to 'all computed digits' (then about 2 x 10^11); this test examines only the first 10^6 digits in each base, so it can refute the claim (a regularity in a prefix would be a regularity) but supports it only for that prefix and that battery. Normality of pi is an open problem and is not what is tested. The published digit file is used for the decimal tests; the independent computation serves to validate it, and supplies the hexadecimal digits.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Pi to 1,000,000 decimal places (Pi-Search page, angio.net)

First 1,000,000 decimal and 1,000,000 hexadecimal digits of pi computed by analysis.py (Chudnovsky series, binary splitting, exact integer arithmetic, 20 guard digits)

OEIS A000796, decimal expansion of pi, b-file (20,000 terms)

OEIS A062964, hexadecimal expansion of pi, b-file (20,000 terms)

20 strings of 1,000,000 uniform random digits per base, numpy PCG64 seed 20261031 (generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The pass condition holds with a wide margin: no p-value below 0.01 (smallest 0.080, the base-16 maximum-periodogram test), and lzma compresses pi's digits to within 0.2 and 0.8 standard deviations of uniform random digit strings in base 10 and base 16. The published file agrees with the independent computation at all 10^6 positions and both OEIS b-files agree at 19,999 positions.

Only the first 10^6 digits in each of two bases were tested, against roughly 2 x 10^11 digits computed when Wolfram wrote and about 10^14 today; the result supports the claim for this prefix and battery and says nothing about normality, which remains unproved.

No positive control (a known non-random digit sequence) was pre-registered for this battery; the same chi-square, serial and compression tests readily reject structured sequences (see e.g. the Champernowne results in wolfram2002-ch10-14), but their power against subtle regularities in pi was not measured here.

Chi-square and normal p-values are asymptotic; every cell has expected count >= 5 (smallest: hexadecimal triples, about 81).
